title: Acids and Bases
seo_title: SSS 2 Chemistry: Acids and Bases Worksheets (WAEC/NECO)
standard_text: The Arrhenius and Lowry–Brønsted theories of acids and bases; conjugate acid–base pairs; ampholytes; acid–base indicators; neutralisation reactions of acids with metal hydroxides, metal oxides and metal carbonates; writing equations for acid–base reactions. (summary of the senior secondary Chemistry curriculum, SSS 2; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 2 Chemistry worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): acids, bases and conjugate pairs, properties of acids and bases, the pH scale and indicators, neutralisation and salts and reactions of acids. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A Lowry–Brønsted acid donates a proton (H⁺).
body_html:
How to think about it

Arrhenius: an acid produces H⁺ (H₃O⁺) ions in water; a base produces OH⁻ ions. Lowry–Brønsted: an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. When an acid donates a proton, it becomes its conjugate base: HCl and Cl⁻ are a conjugate pair. An ampholyte, such as water, can act as an acid or a base.

Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water; acid + metal oxide → salt + water; acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Indicators change colour with pH: litmus, phenolphthalein, methyl orange and bromothymol blue.

Example

Conjugate base of H₂SO₄?

Remove one H⁺

Answer: HSO₄⁻

Example

HCl + NaOH → ?

Acid + base

Answer: NaCl + H₂O

Common mistakes

  • Removing an H atom with its electron for the conjugate base.
  • Thinking all bases dissolve in water (alkalis do).
  • Forgetting CO₂ when an acid reacts with a carbonate.
